requirements.requirement: node2 runs a healthy HTTP service on TCP port 8080
requirements.summary: Executor created appserver.service (python3 http.server) on node2, verified active and responding with content on 8080 both before (cmd-c245b34014bd4873) and after a full node2 reboot (cmd-dedbef54ee1b478d), confirming the service is real and persistent, not just a transient process.

requirements.requirement: node1 (OpenWrt) answers DNS for the shared private network, resolving app.internal to node2's IP
requirements.summary: A dhcp @domain UCI entry mapping app.internal -> 10.100.11.11 was added and committed on node1, dnsmasq restarted, and local nslookup on node1 confirmed the mapping (cmd-f4d54e2551584b3c). The mapping and dnsmasq health were re-verified after a full node1 reboot (cmd-936470b8846a4dce), and node3 could directly query node1's DNS successfully (cmd-c6c028775fd04758).

requirements.requirement: node3 resolves app.internal via node1 by default (no /etc/hosts entry) and reaches node2's HTTP service by that name
requirements.summary: After diagnosing a systemd 229 / resolvconf quirk that reintroduced the stale gateway DNS entry (10.100.11.1) ahead of node1's IP, the executor rewrote node3's systemd-networkd unit to set DNS=10.100.11.10/UseDNS=no and added a persistent nameserver line to /etc/resolvconf/resolv.conf.d/head so node1 sorts first. getent hosts and curl by name succeeded with no /etc/hosts entry both before (cmd-037da515a1474714) and after (cmd-3b600e36caad4ebc) a full node3 reboot, confirming the fix is persistent. The final resolv.conf still lists a stale secondary nameserver (10.100.11.1) which is not authoritative for app.internal, but since node1's address is listed first and resolution succeeded pre- and post-reboot, the working outcome is directly demonstrated.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task are directly demonstrated with pre- and post-reboot evidence: node2 serves HTTP on 8080, node1's dnsmasq authoritatively resolves app.internal to node2's address, and node3 resolves and reaches app.internal by name with no local hosts-file entry. The node3 fix required a non-obvious workaround (resolvconf head-file injection plus a rewritten systemd-networkd unit) to overcome an OS-specific DNS-ordering quirk, but its persistence and correctness were verified both before and after a full reboot. The mandated per-node restart protocol was executed for all three nodes with baseline boot IDs, restart acknowledgements, changed boot IDs, and recovered functional state, though the final global lifecycle snapshot shows an isolated, likely transient failure on the node1 boot-identity probe that slightly undercuts confidence in that node's very last observed state.
limitations: The global after_executor snapshot's node1 boot-identity check failed (return_code 255) even though other node1 probes captured at the same time succeeded, so node1's exact state at the very end of the run could not be fully cross-confirmed from the fixed lifecycle data alone.

The final node3 resolv.conf still contains a duplicate/secondary stale nameserver entry (10.100.11.1) alongside node1's address; correctness currently depends on resolver ordering rather than a fully clean single-nameserver configuration, though this was directly verified to work in both pre- and post-reboot checks.
Two bounded troubleshooting mutations on node3 (drop-in directory, DHCP lease deletion) were reverted/self-healed and are noted for hygiene but did not affect final functional outcomes.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map directly to satisfying the DNS/HTTP requirement or to the mandated restart protocol. Two troubleshooting mutations on node3 were bounded and self-corrected but had no clear causal link to the eventual fix: creation and later removal of a systemd-networkd drop-in directory (cmd-e79e6708a19f4bea, cmd-0dc8cb1bc6034f58, reverted by the rewrite in cmd-bb912fcd429e460b), and a diagnostic stop/delete-leases/restart of systemd-networkd (cmd-a597d7fca98a4725) that removed DHCP lease state before it was naturally refreshed. Neither left residue and neither was destructive or security-weakening, but per the review criteria they still count as unnecessary mutations since they did not contribute to the final working configuration. The final after_executor lifecycle snapshot shows node1's boot-identity probe returning a connection failure (return_code 255) even though the platform, temporary-files, and listening-sockets probes captured at the same timestamp all succeeded for node1, suggesting a transient/single-command hiccup rather than genuine unreachability, but this could not be independently confirmed from the evidence provided.
